title: Why an integrated plan matters
blurb: Explain why producing an integrated project management plan matters: one baseline, aligned plans, shared understanding, control and governance.
question: On a CRM rollout, the project manager wants each workstream (data migration, training, the supplier) to keep its own plan and skip an integrated plan to save time. The sponsor disagrees. Why is producing an integrated project management plan important?

teach.body: Projects are systems: scope, schedule, cost, resources, risk and quality all affect each other. An integrated project management plan (PMP) gives one agreed baseline for delivery, aligns all the plans so a change to one is reflected in the others, builds shared understanding and commitment, provides the basis for monitoring, control and change control, communicates the approach, and supports governance and assurance. In plain English: everyone works from the same page and pulls in the same direction.

What it gives the project
rows: A fixed point to measure progress against
A change in one area is reflected in all
Commitment from sponsor, team and suppliers
Stakeholders and new joiners see how it works
Sponsor approves it; assurance checks against it

teach.h: Pull one thread and the rest move
teach.caption: Because the plans are linked, a change in any one area is assessed for its knock-on effects in all the others.

steps.label: Risk
steps.sub: Go-live now clashes with the year-end freeze

steps.label: Cost
steps.sub: Supplier fees rise; contingency drawn down

teach.caption: With separate plans, each team finds out late. With an integrated PMP, the whole chain is assessed before the change is approved.

teach.body: Once the sponsor approves the PMP, its scope, schedule, cost and quality baselines become the yardstick. Progress reports compare actuals against them, variances trigger action, and change requests are assessed against them. Without one integrated baseline, each team measures against its own assumptions and 'on track' means nothing. Integration also keeps the baseline honest: an approved change updates every affected section, not just one.

teach.h: Separate plans versus one integrated plan

teach.body: Northgate, a software firm, is rolling out a new customer relationship management (CRM) system. The data migration lead planned cut-over for the first weekend of March. The training lead booked trainers for February. The supplier's contract assumed go-live in April. Each plan looked sensible on its own. Pulling them into one integrated PMP exposed the clash in week two, when fixing it cost a few emails rather than a failed go-live.

teach.h: Why it matters in each life cycle

rows.label: Main role
values: Fixes time, cost and ways of working

teach.text: Classic traps: an integrated PMP does NOT guarantee success, replace the business case, or freeze the project. It is a living baseline updated through change control. And a pile of separate plans stapled together is not 'integrated' unless they have been checked against each other and agree.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Make each point a distinct reason: baseline, alignment, shared understanding, control, communication, governance.
Explain the consequence of each, e.g. 'so variances can be measured and acted on early'.
Show integration in action: one change rippling through time, cost, resources and risk.
Where asked, contrast linear (detailed baseline) with iterative (fixed time and cost, flexing scope).
Use the scenario's details rather than generic statements.
An integrated PMP gives one agreed baseline for delivery and control.
It aligns the plans, so a change to one is reflected in all the others.
It builds shared understanding and commitment, and communicates the approach.
It is the basis for monitoring, control and change control, and supports governance and assurance.
It matters in iterative projects too: it fixes time, cost and ways of working while scope flexes.

summary: You can now explain why an integrated project management plan matters: one baseline, aligned plans, shared understanding, a basis for control and change control, and support for governance and assurance. You can also show how a single change ripples through the plan and why integration matters in both linear and iterative projects.

A.q: What is the main reason a project management plan is described as 'integrated'?
options: It joins the subsidiary plans into one consistent whole
It is written jointly by the sponsor and the main supplier
It combines the business case with the benefits register
It merges the project budget into business-as-usual costs
A.why: Integration means the subsidiary plans and management approaches are combined and checked so they are consistent with each other.

whyNot.1: The PM produces the PMP. Suppliers may contribute, but joint authorship is not what 'integrated' means.
whyNot.2: The business case and benefits documents stay separate; the PMP must be consistent with them, not merged with them.
whyNot.3: Integration refers to the project's own plans, not to merging budgets with business as usual.

A.q: Which benefit of an integrated PMP is MOST directly linked to monitoring and control?
options: It removes the need for any formal decision gates
It replaces the need for ongoing stakeholder engagement
It gives one baseline to measure progress against
It fixes the scope so that no change can ever occur
A.why: The approved PMP holds the scope, schedule, cost and quality baselines. Progress is measured against them and variances trigger action.

whyNot.0: Gates remain; the PMP gives the board something to review at them.
whyNot.1: The PMP sets out the engagement approach; it does not replace engagement.
whyNot.3: The plan is updated through change control. It controls change rather than preventing it.

A.q: When the sponsor approves the integrated PMP, what does this mainly give the project?
options: A guarantee that the benefits will be realised
An agreed basis for delivery and control
Freedom to make changes without approval
An end to the need for progress reports
A.why: Approval turns the PMP into the agreed baseline: the basis for delivery, monitoring and change control.

whyNot.0: No plan guarantees benefits; they depend on delivery, adoption and the wider environment.
whyNot.2: After approval, changes go through change control.
whyNot.3: Progress is reported against the approved plan, so reports remain essential.

B.q: A retailer adds a new distribution centre to the scope of its logistics project. Because the plan is integrated, what should happen before the change is approved?
options: Only the scope section is updated; the rest is left as is
The supplier decides whether the change is affordable
The new work is started at once to protect the date
Its effect on time, cost, risk and resources is assessed
B.why: Integration means a change in one area is assessed for its knock-on effects on every other area before a decision is made.

whyNot.0: Updating one section leaves the plans inconsistent, which is exactly what integration prevents.
whyNot.1: Change decisions sit with the appropriate authority (PM, sponsor or board), not the supplier.
whyNot.2: Starting work before assessment and approval bypasses change control.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for producing an integrated PMP?
options: It creates a shared understanding
It removes the need for a business case
It provides a basis for controlling change
It supports governance and assurance
B.why: The business case is still needed because it justifies the project. The PMP must stay consistent with it, not replace it.

whyNot.0: Shared understanding and commitment is a key reason for integration.
whyNot.2: The PMP's baselines are what change requests are assessed against.
whyNot.3: The sponsor approves the PMP, and assurance reviewers check delivery against it.

B.q: On a new school build, the contractor, the designers and the client each refer to a different 'plan' and argue about dates. Which benefit of an integrated PMP is missing?
options: One shared, agreed understanding of the plan
A detailed procurement strategy for suppliers
An independent audit of the business case
A fixed scope that can never be changed
B.why: An integrated PMP gives everyone one agreed version to work from, so dates and commitments are shared.

whyNot.1: A procurement strategy is one part of the plan; it would not resolve competing versions of the dates.
whyNot.2: An audit checks compliance; its absence is not why the parties hold different plans.
whyNot.3: Freezing scope is not a goal of the PMP: change is controlled, not banned.

C.q: A digital agency uses an iterative approach. A developer says: 'We're agile, so we don't need an integrated plan.' What is the best response?
options: Correct: the backlog replaces every other plan
Correct, provided the sponsor agrees in writing
It still fixes time, cost and ways of working
Agile plans must specify every feature up front
C.why: Even in iterative projects an integrated plan fixes time and cost, governance, roles, and the risk and quality approaches, and keeps releases and BAU readiness aligned. The backlog holds the flexible scope.

whyNot.0: The backlog holds the scope only. Risk, quality, roles, governance and transition still need planning.
whyNot.1: Sponsor agreement does not remove the need for an agreed, integrated approach.
whyNot.3: Detailed up-front specification is linear practice; in iterative work scope emerges and is prioritised.

C.q: Which TWO are benefits of producing an integrated PMP? (1) conflicts between plans are found early (2) estimates become fixed and certain (3) assurance reviewers have a baseline to check against (4) change control is no longer needed
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: Integration exposes conflicts early, and it gives governance and assurance an agreed baseline to review.

whyNot.0: Item 2 is wrong: estimates still carry uncertainty and are refined as the project progresses.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: estimates stay uncertain, and change control remains essential.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong: the PMP is the baseline that change control protects.

C.q: On a tower block build, the risk plan assumes the crane is on site in May, but the procurement plan has it arriving in July. What does this most clearly show?
options: The risk appetite has been set far too low
The critical path has been wrongly calculated
The contract should have been fixed price
The plans have not been properly integrated
C.why: Two subsidiary plans contradict each other: the hallmark of plans that have not been integrated and checked against each other.

whyNot.0: Risk appetite is about how much risk is acceptable, not about inconsistent dates.
whyNot.1: The critical path may well be affected, but the root cause is plans that do not agree.
whyNot.2: Contract type would not reconcile two inconsistent plans.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: A family hires an architect, a builder, an electrician and a kitchen fitter for an extension. Each has their own plan. Why does someone need to pull them into one?

blocks.body: The architect's drawings, the builder's programme, the electrician's dates and the kitchen fitter's booking each make sense alone. But the electrician must wire before the plasterer plasters, and the kitchen cannot go in until the plaster has dried. One combined plan shows the dependencies, the true finish date and the total cost. When the family adds a skylight, everyone's dates and costs move together, and nobody turns up on the wrong day.

blocks.h: The combined plan shows the real order
blocks.caption: In their separate plans, the kitchen fitter had booked week 6 and the plasterer week 4, before the wiring. Only the combined plan shows the real sequence.

blocks.text: Integration is not stapling four plans together. It is checking that they agree, so that one change is reflected everywhere it matters.

explain.body: The approved PMP holds the baselines for scope, schedule, cost and quality. Reports compare actual progress against them; variances show where action is needed. Without one baseline there is nothing agreed to measure against.

test.q: Why is a single agreed baseline so important for project control?
options: Variances can only be measured against it
It stops stakeholders asking for any changes
It means the risk register can be closed
It lets the team skip progress reporting
test.why: Control depends on comparing actual progress with an agreed baseline, so variances can be seen and acted on.

whyNot.1: Stakeholders can still request changes; the baseline is what those changes are assessed against.
whyNot.2: Risks are managed throughout; a baseline does not close the risk register.
whyNot.3: Progress is reported against the baseline, so reporting still happens.

explain.body: Because the subsidiary plans are integrated, a change in one is assessed for its effect on the others and every affected section is updated. This prevents the classic failure where one team's plan quietly contradicts another's.

test.q: On a project with an integrated plan, a three-week delay to an equipment delivery is approved. What should follow?
options: Only the procurement section is changed
The sponsor rewrites the business case
The team absorbs it without telling anyone
Linked schedule, cost and risk are updated
test.why: Integration means every affected part of the plan is updated, so the baseline stays consistent.

whyNot.0: Changing one section leaves the other plans out of step.
whyNot.1: The business case is reviewed if the change affects the justification, but a delay first needs the linked plans updated.
whyNot.2: Absorbing changes silently destroys the baseline and the audit trail.

explain.body: One agreed PMP tells everyone how the project will run: the sponsor commits to it, the team knows how work is done and controlled, suppliers see dates and interfaces, and users know when change will land.

test.q: A new workstream lead joins a project halfway through. Why is the integrated PMP especially useful to her?
options: It shows her line manager's priorities
It replaces her induction training
It explains how the project is run
It sets out the organisation's strategy
test.why: The PMP communicates the agreed approach (roles, controls, schedule, reporting), so a new joiner can quickly work in step with everyone else.

whyNot.0: Line-management priorities sit outside the project plan.
whyNot.1: It supports induction to the project but does not replace training.
whyNot.3: Organisational strategy is set elsewhere; the business case links to it.

explain.body: The sponsor approves one integrated plan, gates review it, and assurance reviewers check delivery against it. That gives the board confidence and makes accountability clear.

test.q: How does an integrated PMP support project governance?
options: It lets the PM approve changes of any size
It gives the sponsor one plan to approve
It removes the need for independent assurance
It hands accountability for benefits to the PM
test.why: Governance needs one agreed plan that the sponsor can approve and that gates and assurance can review.

whyNot.0: The PM works within delegated tolerances; larger changes are escalated.
whyNot.2: Assurance remains; the PMP gives it something to check against.
whyNot.3: The sponsor remains accountable for benefits.
